a recent post by Ansh Jain on inequality, I would like to explain Inequality in India in more depth. \n\nMiddle-class or lower-class people don’t live in the same places as rich, which means it’s highly unlikely that you met rich people in early childhood (below Class 5).\n\nIf you meet rich kids after Class 5, it means your parents most likely belong to upper-middle class.\n\nIf you meet rich kids after Class 10, it means your parents most likely belong to middle class.\n\nIf you meet rich kids in college, it means government wants you to meet them, because our education system is non-profit and reservation as representation is mandatory for social justice.\n\nSo, your meeting with rich kids is arranged through the efforts of parents or the government.\n\nI mean, it’s not organic, so it will never be an organic interaction where you can easily understand each other’s contexts.\n\nIn India, education comes under the non-profit sector, that’s why you attend the same schools as the rich in the first place.\n\nUnder the Right to Education Act, 2009, a 25% reservation for underprivileged students in private (unaided/non-minority) schools is mandatory by law. \n\nBut we all know the truth: if parents see kids from poor or marginalised sections of society, they withdraw their children from private schools.\n\nDiscrimination doesn’t only mean “saying bad words”; it also means snatching away people’s rights.\n\nThat’s why inequality is never discussed in urban Indian private schools, and that’s why, when people become adults, they suddenly realise that inequality is everywhere and that it is not one-dimensional but multi-dimensional.\n\nThere is no education related to social justice and DEI.\n\nA classic example is our NCERT books (6th to 10th); there are hardly 4–5 pages regarding caste, gender, and minority issues. \n\nYou won’t find detailed discussions on Jyotiba Phule, Savitribai Phule, Dr. Ambedkar, or the role of the reservation system in decentralizing power in key public institutions (Fabian Socialism) and higher education within an industrial economy by enforcing representation of marginalised communities, while promoting social justice and ensuring that no one group can monopolise the system.\n\nYou also won’t see coverage of the role of the British Labour Party, Fabian Socialism, Sidney Webb, Beatrice Webb, George Bernard Shaw (Nobel, 1925), the London School of Economics, and various British intellectual traditions that shaped ideas of welfare and labor rights in the UK and their contributions in colonies like India, even though India’s labor rights were ultimately achieved through its own indigenous struggles.\n\nDesensitisation toward inequality is deeply rooted in our social structures and institutions, as well as in society at large, which people in urban India don’t want to acknowledge and things will only change when we stop invisibilising it.\n\nPS: We are all Anant Ambani in someone’s story at least in the story of bottom 80 crore living on government’s more : \n\nSocioeconomic Inequality and Census Estimation 2025 (With Caste)\n\nIndia lives in the 1850 and 2025 at the same time.\n\nhttps://www.linkedin.com/posts/yashp2411_socioeconomic-inequality-and-census-estimation-activity-7406889297775292416-8QFV\n\n\nIndian economy and society have been fundamentally built around temple feudalism since 600 CE, which means caste is the core hierarchical structure, so we can use Japan as a benchmark because it was also built on a similar feudal structure.\n\nIndian D = 1850, Japan: People were seeking a stable place so that they did not need to migrate for survival.\nIndian C = 1900, Japan: People were seeking equality in access to basic resources.\nIndian B = 1950, Japan: People were seeking equality and representation.\nIndian A = 1985, Japan: People were seeking progress and social mobility.\n\nIndia is not a monolith and is technically equivalent to a continent in itself, which neglects 90% of its Yash PratapYash Pratap • YouVerified • You Web Dev, System Design, AIWeb Dev, System Design, AI 23h • 23 hours ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn
In a recent post by Ansh Jain on inequality, I would like to explain Inequality in India in more depth.

Middle-class or lower-class people don’t live in the same places as rich, which means it’s highly unlikely that you met rich people in early childhood (below Class 5).

If you meet rich kids after Class 5, it means your parents most likely belong to upper-middle class.

If you meet rich kids after Class 10, it means your parents most likely belong to middle class.

If you meet rich kids in college, it means government wants you to meet them, because our education system is non-profit and reservation as representation is mandatory for social justice.

So, your meeting with rich kids is arranged through the efforts of parents or the government.

I mean, it’s not organic, so it will never be an organic interaction where you can easily understand each other’s contexts.

In India, education comes under the non-profit sector, that’s why you attend the same schools as the rich in the first place.

Under the Right to Education Act, 2009, a 25% reservation for underprivileged students in private (unaided/non-minority) schools is mandatory by law.

But we all know the truth: if parents see kids from poor or marginalised sections of society, they withdraw their children from private schools.

Discrimination doesn’t only mean “saying bad words”; it also means snatching away people’s rights.

That’s why inequality is never discussed in urban Indian private schools, and that’s why, when people become adults, they suddenly realise that inequality is everywhere and that it is not one-dimensional but multi-dimensional.

There is no education related to social justice and DEI.

A classic example is our NCERT books (6th to 10th); there are hardly 4–5 pages regarding caste, gender, and minority issues.

You won’t find detailed discussions on Jyotiba Phule, Savitribai Phule, Dr. Ambedkar, or the role of the reservation system in decentralizing power in key public institutions (Fabian Socialism) and higher education within an industrial economy by enforcing representation of marginalised communities, while promoting social justice and ensuring that no one group can monopolise the system.

You also won’t see coverage of the role of the British Labour Party, Fabian Socialism, Sidney Webb, Beatrice Webb, George Bernard Shaw (Nobel, 1925), the London School of Economics, and various British intellectual traditions that shaped ideas of welfare and labor rights in the UK and their contributions in colonies like India, even though India’s labor rights were ultimately achieved through its own indigenous struggles.

Desensitisation toward inequality is deeply rooted in our social structures and institutions, as well as in society at large, which people in urban India don’t want to acknowledge and things will only change when we stop invisibilising it.

PS: We are all Anant Ambani in someone’s story at least in the story of bottom 80 crore living on government’s food.

Indian B = 1950, Japan: People were seeking equality and representation.
Indian A = 1985, Japan: People were seeking progress and social mobility.

Socioeconomic Inequality and Census Estimation 2025 (With Caste)

https://www.linkedin.com/posts/yashp2411_socioeconomic-inequality-and-census-estimation-activity-7406889297775292416-8QFV?utm_source=social_share_send&utm_medium=android_app&rcm=ACoAACxrlNsBn9c2b7b2lZ8UK2ckDiW-YTjaB0I&utm_campaign=copy_link



Indian economy and society have been fundamentally built around temple feudalism since 600 CE, which means caste is the core hierarchical structure, so we can use Japan as a benchmark because it was also built on a similar feudal structure.

Indian D = 1850, Japan: People were seeking a stable place so that they did not need to migrate for survival.
Indian C = 1900, Japan: People were seeking equality in access to basic resources.
Indian B = 1950, Japan: People were seeking equality and representation.
Indian A = 1985, Japan: People were seeking progress and social mobility.

India is not a monolith and is technically equivalent to a continent in itself, which neglects 90% of its population.
